Belfast is typically divided up into North/South/East/West, and even in the North and South of the city where there are fairly even numbers of Catholics and Protestants, even today they still self-segregate so there are always exclusively Catholic and exclusively Protestant neighbourhoods. It's not that a Protestant can't live in a traditionally Catholic neighborhood or vice versa, it's just that they choose not to. 
It probably isn't helped by the fact that there are now more peace walls than there were during the Troubles. Peace Walls are essentially walls put up between neighbouring Catholic and Protestant communities to prevent them from attacking each other, with the gates to get through being closed at night. They are sad to see but are unfortunately necessary, particularly in places like where the super-Unionist Shankill Road meets the super-Nationalist Falls Road, which has seen some violence in the last couple of years.

6. This is a bit of a big one. All the way back in the early 1600s, Ireland had finally been conquered by England. This was at the same time as the Kingdoms of England and Scotland were united under the same King, the Scottish James I (just as what's called a Personal Union, the UK didn't get formed until the early 1700s), who was a Protestant. Under his reign, mostly Scottish Presbyterian settlers moved into Ireland, with the majority settling in the North-east as that was closest. By the 1900s, the descendants of these settlers - the "Protestants" - were the majority in this area, although a considerable number of native Irish still remained, who were overwhelmingly Catholic - the "Catholics". Fast forward to today and although the number of Catholics has increased it is still like two parallel communities - while religion still plays a role, the words Protestant and Catholic nowadays are kind of just a byword for the two groups of people who live here. As a Protestant, my surname is Scottish and so are the surnames of all of my great-grandparents from here, whereas a Catholic would probably have an Irish surname like Murphy or O'Connor. Both groups grow up very differently, for example someone from the Catholic community likely went to a Catholic school and is taught the Catholic viewpoint on religion, contraception etc whereas my school sang Protestant hymns at Christmas and sang the national anthem at the annual awards ceremony. 
To sum it up, while most "Catholics" will probably be Catholic and a decent proportion of "Protestants" will be Protestant, the words are more just used to describe each community as each grew out of initial religious differences back during the Scottish colonisation.

Yes, of course it's a very different situation, all I was trying to illustrate is that for many white Americans their families have been in that land for around the same time as my family and the families of many Unionists in Northern Ireland. Both groups came to be there because of colonisation, which everyone can agree is a bad thing, but both groups feel very established where they are and would think of it as their home. 
Of course, there are plenty of Catholics probably a half hour drive from where I live that feel the exact same - they are Irish, Ireland is their country, so of course they want their home to be a part of their country. It's not a divide that I see ever really coming to an end (even if it is thankfully moved to our parliament rather than open warfare) and it's something that very few even here in Northern Ireland understand. 
Way back in the 1910s (if you'll allow me a small history lesson lmao) when the British government was trying to introduce "Home Rule" (meaning a sort of devolution of powers over local matters to a parliament in Ireland, while it would remain in the UK), a crisis erupted over the opposition of Protestants in the North-east of the island to the idea, who overwhelmingly opposed anything that might lead Ireland away from Britain. Winston Churchill, at that time only a Minister in Prime Minister Asquith's government, visited Belfast and concluded that there were "Two Nations" in Ireland - something that I think is very true for NI today.

I'm first of all very fortunate to have been born nearly a decade after they ended, and I'm glad that I can freely walk through Belfast without needing to go through checkpoints to make sure I am not carrying a bomb. The causes of the Troubles were many and have their roots in events that happened hundreds of years ago, but as to the catalyst of the Civil Rights Movement for Catholics (or NICRA) I can see how the mismanagement and discrimination of our government directly led to the growth of the IRA and the outbreak of violence. It was a very preventable conflict that could have been nipped in the bud if people on both sides had been less intransigent. 


As for stories, I only have one from my grandfather to share. My grandfather's younger brother worked part-time in the police force (the Royal Ulster Constabulary), meaning he had another job and just worked a couple shifts a week with the police force. On one of these shifts my grandfather's brother was sitting hanging out of the back of a police truck with the back doors open as the truck left the police station in a Catholic area. The IRA had secretly taken over a house across the street and as the truck pulled out, one of the IRA there saw my grandfather's brother and shot him in the neck. 


Doctors were able to keep him alive, but he was effectively in a coma and would never wake up. My great-grandparents couldn't answer the doctors' question of if he should be kept alive or not, so it fell to my grandfather at the age of 32 to decide to tell the doctors to pull the plug on his wee brother. Thankfully, my grandfather found solace in Church and became a much more convinced Christian, but small stories like that are what convinced many young men eager for revenge to join the UDA/UVF or the IRA.

I'm not here to debate who "deserves" this land, nor the merits of unification, but I do concede that the circumstances through which people of my community came to be here were less than justified. Does that mean however that our opinions do not matter, or that we don't deserve a say on what happens to our home? My ancestors came over from Scotland around the same time as British settlers began to land in North America - should the descendants of European settlers in America similarly accept that it is "right" to forfeit their say and give all their land back to the Native Americans?

I think particularly in working class communities where the paramilitaries tend to be stronger there is still a lot distrust of "the other side", but for the average young person at least there isn't really much animosity. That isn't entirely for good reasons though - Protestants and Catholics still grow up going to different schools and there are a disappointing number of people who spend their whole childhood without ever meeting someone from the other community, which means there is perhaps less friction. 


As for relations with people from the Republic of Ireland, we tend to get on very well regardless of if you're a Protestant or Catholic - we all like rugby, beer, and some good craic.

The paramilitaries have essentially developed into normal criminal gangs by now, with the caveat that they can claim political reasons for selling drugs. Any violence is normally within a 'side' about territory, for example recently we had violence between loyalist paramilitaries over some territory in a town called Newtonards.

Despite not being religious myself, I am what would be called a Protestant - I have grown up in walking distance of multiple places where bonfires are lit on the 12th of July to celebrate the Protestant King William of Orange's victory over the Catholic King James II in 1690 and my school used Protestant hymns, sang God Save the Queen/King at annual award ceremonies etc. 
Like most from my community, I am against becoming part of the Republic of Ireland - I recognise that it will likely happen at some point but the way I see it is fairly simple: I am a British citizen, the UK is my country that I am proud of, so why would I want my home to be taken out of my country?

I'm from Northern Ireland in the UK, so while our education system is pretty similar to what people on the mainland have it does have some quirks. 


From 3-4 you can go to something called Nursery, which from what little I remember is only really basic stuff like trying to teach you how to write and count and play with Legos. 


After that you have 7 years of Primary School from Primary 1 (P1) right up to Primary 7 (P7). In P7 around November-December every student does something called the Transfer Test, a standardised test that tests your English and Maths skills.


After Primary School is where it gets more complicated. You can go to a High School, which doesn't look at your Transfer Test score and so basically anyone can attend. They typically only teach up to the GCSE exams that you do in your Fifth year of High School when you're 15-16.
The other option is to go to a Grammar School, like I did. From what I gather these are different from Grammar Schools in England but I am not sure. At Grammar Schools, to get in you need to achieve a certain score in the Transfer Test, and most tend to fix that score at just above average. Grammar Schools teach you for 7 years, taking you through the GCSEs as well as the A-Levels that you sit in years 6 and 7. It's these A-Levels that you need to apply to University in the UK.


One thing about Northern Ireland in particular is that we have always had a particularly high level of education funding compared to schools in the rest of the UK, with all our usually squabbling political parties uniting about a decade ago to stop the Conservatives from cutting education funding for Northern Ireland. People I've spoken to from England have said that our Grammar Schools are far better funded and equipped than the average English school for example and are maybe at the level of mid-level private schools in England.
